derivation_notes: Each input is represented by a nonnegative Hill occupancy factor, as commonly used for saturable biochemical activation. Their product models coincident gating at translation initiation, giving a rate that is nondecreasing in either input and bounded above by v_max.

domain_mechanisms.description: finite receptor occupancy or saturating signal transduction

scenario_text: Cells are measured under independently sampled amino-acid and growth-factor conditions, and protein synthesis is recorded before slower changes in cell number occur. Growth-factor signaling activates a kinase-controlled translation program, while amino-acid availability controls the capacity of that program. The baseline output is an instantaneous translation rate rather than a time-evolving protein pool.

derivation_notes: The parent assumes amino-acid availability only multiplies a fixed growth-factor Hill response. Here amino-acid sufficiency also lowers the effective growth-factor half-activation level through the same bounded amino-acid capacity factor, yielding a monotone, bounded non-separable interaction without adding a new input or state.
change_summary: Relaxed the assumption of independent multiplicative gating by making growth-factor sensitivity depend on amino-acid status. This changes the scored static mapping because G titration curves can shift left at higher A instead of differing only by amplitude.

assumption_audit.released_assumption: Growth-factor-dependent kinase activation and amino-acid-dependent translational capacity combine as independent multiplicative gates with fixed growth-factor sensitivity parameters K_G and n_G that do not depend on amino-acid status.
assumption_audit.mechanism: Amino-acid sufficiency can condition the responsiveness of translation initiation to growth-factor signaling by reducing the effective growth-factor threshold once nutrient-dependent translational competence is established.
assumption_audit.parent_reduction: The successor reduces to the parent when alpha_A = 0, so the effective growth-factor threshold becomes K_G and the G response reverts to the fixed Hill function.

response_change.parent_relation: The current mapping is a product of two independent Hill saturations, so growth-factor signaling rescales translation by the same normalized factor at all amino-acid levels and amino acids rescale translation by the same normalized factor at all growth-factor levels.
response_change.child_relation: Relax the assumption of independent multiplicative gating by allowing amino-acid availability to shift the effective growth-factor sensitivity of the kinase-controlled translation program, creating a non-separable monotone interaction between A and G.
response_change.observable_effect: When G is titrated at fixed low versus high A, the child shows a different apparent growth-factor threshold or steepness across those amino-acid conditions, whereas the parent can only change the amplitude through the amino-acid prefactor.

evolution_contract.activation_condition: Observable when A is varied across sub-saturating to near-saturating levels while G is also swept through its activation range, especially for A around or below K_A and G around K_G; the effect vanishes when A is fully saturating or uniformly very low over all samples.
evolution_contract.train_hidden_contrast: In training, paired G titrations at several fixed A levels already reveal whether normalized G-response curves collapse after amplitude rescaling; in holdout, the same mechanism extends to intermediate or higher A where the shift in apparent G sensitivity becomes stronger or weaker but remains monotone and bounded.
evolution_contract.continuation_path: The parent law is recovered in the limit where amino-acid availability no longer modulates growth-factor sensitivity, i.e. the interaction parameter tends to zero so the effective G-response reverts to a fixed Hill function with constant K_G and n_G.
evolution_contract.domain_mechanism: nutrient-dependent shift of growth-factor sensitivity in translation initiation
evolution_contract.scientific_mechanism: Amino-acid sufficiency can condition the responsiveness of translation initiation to growth-factor signaling, for example by making kinase-driven activation more effective once nutrient-dependent translational competence is established, yielding an amino-acid-dependent growth-factor threshold without violating monotonicity or boundedness.
evolution_contract.difficulty_rationale: This is structurally harder than a coefficient-only correction because the G half-activation is now an explicit bounded function of A, so the normalized G-response shape depends on amino-acid condition rather than being globally collapsible by amplitude rescaling.
evolution_contract.assumption_before: Growth-factor-dependent kinase activation and amino-acid-dependent translational capacity combine as independent multiplicative gates with fixed growth-factor sensitivity parameters K_G and n_G that do not depend on amino-acid status.
evolution_contract.assumption_after: Amino-acid status modulates the effective growth-factor threshold through a bounded saturation law, so growth-factor responsiveness depends on nutrient-dependent translational competence.
evolution_contract.parent_reduction: Setting alpha_A = 0 recovers the parent expression exactly.
evolution_contract.observable_signature: Parent response relationship: at fixed A, v_translation versus G has exactly the same normalized Hill shape because A only multiplies the curve. Child change: A alters the G-response shape itself by lowering the effective growth-factor threshold through a saturating amino-acid factor. Distinguishing condition: vary G over its activation range while holding A fixed first at a low-but-nonzero level and then at a higher sub-saturating level; compare normalized G-response curves. In the parent, one shared parameter set forces those normalized curves to coincide, differing only in maximum height. In the child, the higher-A condition exhibits a left-shift in G responsiveness. This is observable when both inputs span non-saturating regimes, especially A around or below K_A and G around K_G, and it changes the scored static input-output mapping itself, not merely an auxiliary trajectory.
evolution_contract.shortcut_blocked: A single refit of the parent parameters cannot reproduce different normalized G-response thresholds across A conditions because its separable product enforces the same function of G at every A up to an overall multiplicative factor. Refitting all existing parent parameters can change the common amplitude law and one shared G-response shape, but cannot generate amino-acid-dependent left-shifts or amino-acid-dependent G-curve steepness changes with one parameter set across those conditions.

evolution_plan.activation_condition: Observable when A is varied across sub-saturating to near-saturating levels while G is also swept through its activation range, especially for A around or below K_A and G around K_G; the effect vanishes when A is fully saturating or uniformly very low over all samples.
evolution_plan.train_hidden_contrast: In training, paired G titrations at several fixed A levels already reveal whether normalized G-response curves collapse after amplitude rescaling; in holdout, the same mechanism extends to intermediate or higher A where the shift in apparent G sensitivity becomes stronger or weaker but remains monotone and bounded.
evolution_plan.continuation_path: The parent law is recovered in the limit where amino-acid availability no longer modulates growth-factor sensitivity, i.e. the interaction parameter tends to zero so the effective G-response reverts to a fixed Hill function with constant K_G and n_G.
evolution_plan.gap_statement: The model assumes amino-acid supply only sets a multiplicative capacity ceiling and does not alter how much growth-factor signaling is needed to engage translation, omitting plausible nutrient-dependent tuning of growth-factor efficacy at the initiation machinery.
evolution_plan.baseline_assumption: Growth-factor-dependent kinase activation and amino-acid-dependent translational capacity combine as independent multiplicative gates with fixed growth-factor sensitivity parameters K_G and n_G that do not depend on amino-acid status.
evolution_plan.scientific_mechanism: Amino-acid sufficiency can condition the responsiveness of translation initiation to growth-factor signaling, for example by making kinase-driven activation more effective once nutrient-dependent translational competence is established, yielding an amino-acid-dependent growth-factor threshold without violating monotonicity or boundedness.
evolution_plan.rationale: Parent response: at any fixed A, v_translation versus G has exactly the same normalized Hill shape because A only multiplies the curve. Proposed child change: A alters the G-response shape itself, such as shifting the effective growth-factor threshold with nutrient status. Distinguishing condition: vary G over its activation range while holding A fixed first at a low-but-nonzero level and then at a higher sub-saturating level; compare normalized G-response curves. In the parent, one shared parameter set forces those normalized curves to coincide, differing only in maximum height. In the child, the higher-A condition can exhibit a left-shift or altered curvature in G responsiveness, reflecting stronger growth-factor efficacy once amino-acid capacity is available. This is scientifically admissible because both nutrient and growth-factor signaling converge on translation initiation, and the measurement is instantaneous so no new state is needed. The effect is observable only when both inputs span non-saturating regimes; if all A values are either near zero or fully saturating, the interaction is hard to identify. This changes the scored static input-output mapping itself, not merely an auxiliary trajectory.
